messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Raymond is a 61-year-old married bus driver who presented for psychological assessment following a prolonged period of distress he had largely kept hidden from his family and colleagues. He is a broad-shouldered, quietly spoken man of Canadian descent who has lived in the same mid-sized American city for over thirty years. He came to the intake appointment alone, arriving early and choosing a seat in the waiting room that faced the door.

Approximately two years before seeking help, Raymond was part of a humanitarian convoy that crossed into a conflict zone during a family visit to relatives abroad. The convoy was stopped at an unofficial checkpoint, and Raymond, along with several others including a younger male cousin, was detained and held for eleven days. During that time he was subjected to systematic physical abuse — beatings that followed a rhythm he came to dread, conducted in a concrete room lit by a single overhead bulb. What remained seared into his memory was not the pain itself but a specific sequence: the sound of boots on a stone corridor in the minutes before the door opened, and the moment he looked at his cousin's face and saw the younger man's terror reflected back at him. Raymond had been positioned closer to the guards and had, on more than one occasion, been used as the primary subject while his cousin was made to watch. He survived. His cousin survived. But Raymond left that room carrying a certainty that he had not done enough — that he had not thrown himself further into harm's way, had not spoken up at the right moments, had not found some act of will that might have spared his cousin any part of what they both endured.

In the months after returning home, Raymond resumed driving his bus route — the 7:15 morning run through the downtown corridor and back. For a time, the routine seemed to help. But the cab of the bus became its own kind of terrain. On mornings when a passenger boarded wearing heavy work boots and walked down the aisle, Raymond's chest would tighten and his hands would go rigid on the wheel. The sound of footsteps on the metal floor — particularly a certain deliberate, unhurried rhythm — produced a physical response he could not override: his heart rate spiked, his vision narrowed, and for several seconds the fluorescent interior of the bus and the concrete walls of that room seemed to occupy the same space. He never spoke of these episodes to his dispatcher or to the passengers. He simply gripped the wheel and drove.

At home, the nights became a separate problem. Raymond found himself lying awake long after his wife had fallen asleep, listening. He could not have explained, precisely, what he was listening for — only that the house at night felt provisional in a way it never had before, as though its walls offered a conditional safety that could be withdrawn. He began sleeping with the bedroom door slightly ajar so he could hear the full range of sounds from the hallway and the front of the house. His wife noticed but attributed it to age and stress. Raymond did not correct her.

His memory of the detention itself remained fractured in ways that disturbed him. Certain moments were available to him with a clarity that felt almost physical — the grain of the concrete wall, the particular quality of the light — while other stretches were simply absent, blank intervals he could not account for. When he attempted to reconstruct the full sequence of events, the terror he had felt in that room returned with it, not as recollection but as something present and immediate. He had come to avoid thinking about the event directly for this reason, though the fragments arrived anyway, unbidden.

What finally brought Raymond to seek help was a near-miss on his route in the spring: he had momentarily lost his concentration after a passenger's footsteps triggered a physical response, and the bus drifted toward a curb before he corrected. No one was hurt. No one noticed. But Raymond sat in the depot afterward for forty minutes, shaking, and understood that he could not continue managing this alone. He came to the first session hoping, above all, to be able to do his job without endangering the people in his care — and dreading that the process of treatment would require him to confront, fully and without gaps, everything he believes he failed to do.
